svg.title: GARCH vs Stochastic Volatility
svg.desc: GARCH variance is computed from past observations; SV variance is a latent state with its own noise, which turns the likelihood into an integration problem.
svg.text: A variance computed from the past vs a latent state that moves on its own
A deterministic function of past data
A latent state with its own noise
Two — an observation shock and a state shock
Requires integrating out a latent variable
The discrete counterpart of the Heston model
Variance is computed from data (one noise)
Given the information set, the variance is a single number
The variance has its own shock (two noises)
h is unobserved, so it must be inferred
The variance comes out as a single number
A conditional variance, with no interval
The same data always reproduces the same value
The variance itself has a distribution
Reports uncertainty about the volatility estimate as well
GARCH variance is computed from past data; SV variance is a latent state.
That difference turns the likelihood into an integral and pushes estimation toward MCMC and particle filters.
Using log y² as the observation gives a non-Gaussian state-space model —
Kalman approximations or particle filters apply directly
Next: measuring volatility directly at high frequency — realized volatility vs GARCH.
